A partial digestion of the HRT counterexample
6 August, 2026 in
expository
,
math.CA
| Tags:
HRT conjecture
,
time-frequency analysis
| by
Terence Tao
A function
of one variable can be translated in space by a spatial shift
to obtain a new function
and also modulated in frequency by a frequency shift
to obtain a new function
One can compose these two operations to obtain a time-frequency shift:
(This can be viewed of as a portion of the
Weyl representation of the Heisenberg group
, but we will not adopt a representation-theoretic perspective here.)
Some functions obey finite linear relations between their time-frequency shifts. For instance, a sinusoid
obeys the relation
However, the Heil-Ramanathan-Topiwala (HRT) conjecture states that once one imposes some reasonable decay condition on
, no such relations exist:
Conjecture 1 (HRT conjecture)
If
is non-zero, then there is no relation of the form
for some distinct points
and some coefficients
, not all zero.
A special case of the HRT conjecture, which was also open, makes the additional assumption that
was Schwartz.
Many positive results towards this conjecture were known. I will mention only a few here. There is a
result of Linnell
that the conjecture is true if
lie in a translate of a discrete subgroup of
; this (together with an argument handling the collinear case) establishes all cases where
, and several partial results involving the
cases are also known. The conjecture is also known if
decays at a suitably super-exponential rate, by
work of Bownik and Speegle
.
I was aware of this conjecture through various talks and conversations with colleagues, and even briefly tried my hand at it for a while, though not with particularly serious effort (or progress). It was thus a nice surprise to see that it has
just been resolved by Faulhuber, Petersen, van Velthoven, and Voigtlaender
, even in the Schwartz case:
Theorem 2
There exist complex numbers
, not all zero, distinct points
, and a non-zero Schwartz function
such that
It is perhaps unsurprising in this current era that this result is AI-assisted. However, I think the authors have disclosed their AI use responsibly, with the final arguments written by hand with a readable overview of the argument, as well as proper discussion of methods, relation to past literature, and other independent numerical checks on the result.
The negative result lies only a little beyond the positive results:
is now increased to
, and all but one of the points
lie in (a translate of) a discrete subgroup of
(in fact the explicit subgroup
is used). The functions constructed are smooth and rapidly decaying, but not analytic or super-exponentially decaying, which would start being in conflict with the known positive results.
In addition to AI being used to come up with the initial proof strategy, a more traditional numerical computation was used to verify one step of the argument.
I have not had the time to do a full digestion of the result, but (after reading the introduction, and
using a little AI assistance of my own
) I was able to understand the main ideas at a high level. The first few reductions are relatively standard. Setting
and
, one can view the problem as one of solving an eigenvalue problem
The time-frequency shifts
are chosen to lie in a translate of the discrete subgroup
by a certain irrational shift
. If one was working in the shifts of a standard lattice
, it would be natural to work with the
Zak transform
of
, but it turns out that the approach does not quite work when doing this for topological reasons (relating to the fact that scalar quasiperiodic functions of mean zero are forced to have zeroes), and so the authors used the slightly denser lattice instead
, which relates to a vector-valued version of the Zak transform taking values in
rather than
. Applying this transform, the eigenvalue problem can be transformed by standard calculations to a “vector cocycle problem”
where
is a non-zero smooth quasiperiodic vector-valued function,
is an irrational shift
, and
is a certain explicit
matrix-valued function depending on the choices of
,
, and
.
How to solve this equation? The motivating scenario here is if the matrix function
was replaced by a rank one function
for some smooth vector-valued function
of unit magnitude. Then one could solve the equation by taking
and
. It is not possible to make the function
exactly of this form, but through some numerical computation and clever AI-assisted guesswork, the authors were able to find a choice of
and
, and
that made
approximately equal
to a rank one function
of this form, in fact getting a uniform estimate
As it turns out, such an approximation is sufficient to run a contraction mapping argument to find a solution to a variant of
(1)
, namely
for some smooth
and
. (Here it was important to get the operator norm bound below
; they are barely able to do this, with a numerically obtained bound of
, though this bound might not be optimal.)
The main remaining obstacle is that the “eigenvalue function”
is varying in the parameter
rather than constant. (This issue was, by the way, anticipated to some extent in
previous work of Demeter
, who observed that eigenfunctions of the almost Matthieu discrete Schrödinger operator gave a near-miss counterexample to the HRT conjecture, but with an eigenvalue that depended on an auxiliary phase shift parameter rather than constant.) However, if one was able to solve the scalar cocycle equation
for some smooth
, then one could solve the equation
(1)
by setting
. The approach to solve
(2)
is standard: take logarithms, apply a Fourier transform, and then divide out by the multiplier associated to the
shift. This can cause a well-known “small divisor” problem (which arises in various dynamical contexts, such as in the
KAM theorem
) if
behaves too much like a rational vector, but the standard resolution to this is to select a shift
that obeys good Diophantine approximation properties. For the purposes of numerics the authors selected an extremely concrete shift, namely
but I get the impression that the exact choice here was not crucial for the argument, and that many other irrational algebraic numbers could have worked here.

This was one of the topics I discussed in my
conversation with an AI
. The specific construction used would be difficult to directly reduce in size, but it seems likely that some variant of the construction could lower
slightly from its current value of
, though it seems unlikely that the lowest theoretically possible value
would be attainable by this method.
In the opposite direction, it appears that if one is fine with disproving the HRT conjecture with a large unspecified value of
, that one can adapt the arguments in the preprint to do this without any numerical computation whatsoever, roughly speaking by developing a Stone-Weierstrass type result that asserts that the set of all possible matrix functions
(with unspecified
) is dense enough that one can approximate any given rank one candidate
uniformly to any desired accuracy. In fact one does not even need the full strength of the Stone-Weierstrass theorem; a standard Fourier series expansion, followed by a truncation, is sufficient. I used an AI to generate a quick sketch of this variant of the argument
here
.

6 August, 2026 at 5:49 pm
Vignon Oussa
Professor Tao, thank you for this very helpful digestion. I believe your qualification “by this method” identifies exactly the relevant difficulty. A direct compression of the one-step rank-one approximation appears implausible with only three Weyl terms.
The four-point candidate I have been studying attempts to evade that obstruction rather than overcome it directly. Its one-step symbol is
A(x,ω) = I + (3/5)e^{-πiω}D + (3/5)e^{πix}S.
It is not uniformly close to rank one. Indeed, at x=ω=1/2 one has A* A=(43/25)I, so its operator-norm distance from every rank-one matrix is √43/5, far above the 1/3 perturbative threshold.
The proposed mechanism instead uses long-block domination. Outward-rounded interval calculations give, uniformly in z,
σ₂(P₁₆(z))/σ₁(P₁₆(z)) < 10⁻³,
together with a consecutive-block junction bound greater than 1/4. The invariant line is therefore produced by sixteen-step dominated dynamics rather than by one-step proximity to a prescribed rank-one transporter. A two-gauge half-plane calculation is then used to control the multiplier winding, after which the cubic Diophantine cohomological argument produces the eigenfunction.
This leads to the proposed relation
[I+(3/5)ρ(1,0)+(3/5)ρ(0,1/2)]ρ(ζ)g=λg,
where ζ=(∛2−1,(∛4−1)/2), giving four shifts after including the eigenvalue term.
Because a four-point counterexample would be a minimal and very surprising result, I am treating the manuscript as provisional pending independent specialist checking. The complete Arb verification supplement is available
here
, and the partial Lean companion is available
here
. The Lean file verifies many finite algebraic bridges but is not an end-to-end formalization.
I would be especially grateful for scrutiny of the passage from the block-dominated splitting to the globally sewn one-step invariant section, and of the subsequent winding and cohomological steps. Thus, as I presently understand it, your skepticism remains correct for the one-step approximation architecture, while the candidate uses a different, long-block dynamical mechanism.

You highlight in your post that the authors responsibly disclosed their AI use, and as a consequence I got curious and had a look, making me then ponder about the question of whether expecting such disclosures is actually helpful. I understand that naming a tool precisely can be crucial in research, for the purpose of making the obtained results reproducible by others. But AI acknowledgements in math seem not to help much in this direction. If all sources of used ideas have been correctly and carefully cited (which may be hard work in the case of AI assistance, as AI tools could omit origins of ideas) and if all colleagues who gave some useful input have been acknowledged (at least those who wanted to be acknowledged), I feel it could be already sufficient. In my working country, it can be quite difficult to get access to strong AI tools for research, and seeing all these disclosures recently I don’t really know what to think about them. Do papers without AI disclosures now receive increasing skepticism (like people thinking along the lines of “they most likely used AI in an essential way but just hide it”)? What about authors who cannot afford good AI tools, should they consider making up fake AI disclosures just for the sake of not looking suspicious? (of course the answer to that one should be a clear no, but I was still wondering about this). And on the contrary, could honest AI disclosures (even in the case of very minor AI use) be actually hurtful for the careers of unexperienced and young authors (say with their first paper in 2026 or later)? Sorry for drifting off topic.
Reply
7 August, 2026 at 7:17 pm
Terence Tao
My view is that AI disclosure is consistent with the scientific principle of disclosing one’s research methodology, which I believe to be good practice even if not directly reproducible. For instance, knowing that a certain problem is amenable to AI assistance provides useful information that related problems might also benefit from such assistance. Also, it is possible that authors might be willing to supply prompts or other information about their use of AI upon request.
I have also seen negative AI disclosures, in that the authors declared for instance that they tried using AI tools but did not obtain useful output from them. This I think is also useful information (and it would be more broadly useful in general to have more normalized reporting of negative results).
I will also note that disclosure of tool use is one of the recommendations of the
Leiden declaration
.
